newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin to complete govt changes ahead of strikes.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin to complete govt changes ahead of strikes.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin, back in the Kremlin after a summit meeting with U.S. President Bill Clinton, puts the finishing touches on Monday to a government shake-up he hopes will help defuse rising social tensions.

But trade unions have vowed to press on with a day of strikes on Thursday to protest against big delays in payment of wages and pensions and the Russian authorities have begun beefing up security arrangements to forestall possible trouble.

Yeltsin, whose talks with Clinton in Helsinki focused on the thorny issue of NATO's eastward expansion, will meet other foreign leaders this week in a clear sign that he is firmly back in control after months of illness.

Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen were both due in Moscow on Monday, underscoring the importance of Russia's ties with Asia as it continues its war of words with the West over NATO and other issues.

Last week Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said NATO's plans to admit former communist countries in eastern and central Europe could force Moscow to review its foreign policy and strengthen links with China, India and Iran.
Russian newspapers picked up this theme again over the weekend in response to Clinton's refusal in Helsinki to modify NATO's expansion plans.
At their summit Clinton and Yeltsin agreed to differ over NATO's plans and push ahead with a charter defining a new relationship between Moscow and the Atlantic alliance.

Yeltsin dropped a key Russian demand that the charter should be legally binding and promised to minimise differences over NATO expansion. Moscow still opposes NATO's plans to admit members from central and eastern Europe, saying they are a threat to its own security.

On Sunday Grigory Yavlinsky, who heads the liberal Yabloko faction in the State Duma lower house of parliament, told Interfax news agency that Yeltsin had effectively said yes in the Finnish capital to NATO enlargement.
"But it is not NATO expansion itself that poses the real threat to Russia but the reasons that led to the expansion," Interfax quoted Yavlinsky as saying.
He said these included Russia's political instability, the failure of economic reform and chaos in its under-funded and demoralised armed forces.

These issues top the agenda of Yeltsin's newly restructured government and its two leading lights, first deputy prime ministers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov, signalled over the weekend that, like Yeltsin, they were fighting fit and ready to press on with the next stage of reform.

"The president convinced me to take this post," Nemtsov, a liberal, told NTV commercial television on Sunday. "The president made clear he could not bear the current situation any more. He is very firm and will go down in history as a creator."

Speaking to Russian public television, Chubais, who is also finance minister in the new cabinet, ruled out the possibility of a coalition government, saying the answers to Russia's problems should not be held up by party squabbles.

Chubais, architect of Russia's post-communist privatisation programme, is loathed by the communists who dominate the Duma. They are backing Thursday's national day of action and have been critical of Yeltsin's government reshuffle.

Chubais, 41, said tackling non-payment of wages and pensions was the "top priority of the government". The government has in the past blamed tax dodgers for the arrears, which affect millions of workers and often stretch back many months.
Author and former dissident Alexander Solzhenitsyn weighed into the fray on Sunday, saying neglect of education and research would soon reduce Russia to Third World status.
"Our schools, science are rotting away. In two or three years' time we will have become like some second-rate African country," Solzhenitsyn told NTV commercial television.
"There is a terrifying split in society...We are in great danger now," said the ascetic author, who has become a stern critic of the new capitalist Russia.
